cards.question_text: Which term describes the system by which an organization directs and controls security through accountability, defined roles, and risk-based decision-making?
choices: Security governance — it sets strategic direction and oversight, distinct from management which executes
Security management — it involves day-to-day operational decisions only
Security operations — it refers to monitoring and incident response activities
Security architecture — it describes the technical design of security controls
cards.answer: Security governance — it sets strategic direction and oversight, distinct from management which executes
cards.explanation_correct: Security governance is the framework of leadership, accountability, and oversight that aligns security with business objectives. It defines who is responsible, sets risk appetite, and ensures the board/leadership has visibility. Management is the execution layer — implementing the policies and controls that governance directs. This separation ensures strategic oversight is not lost in tactical operations.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B confuses governance with management — management executes, governance directs. Option C is security operations (SOC activities), a subset of management. Option D is security architecture, which is a technical design discipline, not the governance framework.

cards.question_text: In the document hierarchy, which of the following correctly orders documents from most authoritative (mandatory, high-level) to least authoritative (optional, advisory)?
choices: Policy → Standard → Baseline → Guideline
Guideline → Baseline → Standard → Policy
Standard → Policy → Guideline → Baseline
Baseline → Guideline → Policy → Standard
cards.answer: Policy → Standard → Baseline → Guideline
cards.explanation_correct: Policies are mandatory, high-level directives from management. Standards are mandatory and specify technical requirements to comply with the policy. Baselines are mandatory minimum security configurations (e.g., CIS benchmarks). Guidelines are optional, recommended practices that provide flexibility. This hierarchy ensures enforceable expectations cascade from strategic to tactical levels while allowing discretion where appropriate.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B reverses the hierarchy entirely. Option C swaps policy and standard — policies are higher-level than standards. Option D places baseline and guideline above policy, which is incorrect — policies are the top of the hierarchy.

cards.question_text: A new CISO joins a company and discovers that the security policy was last updated 6 years ago, references technologies no longer in use, and does not mention cloud services or mobile devices. The policy is still technically 'in force.' What is the most appropriate governance action?
choices: Initiate a comprehensive policy review and update cycle, establish a recurring review schedule (e.g., annual), and ensure the updated policy covers current technologies, cloud, BYOD, and emerging threats
Delete the old policy and operate without one until a new one can be written from scratch over the next year
Keep the existing policy since it is still technically in force and add a separate cloud security document alongside it
Delegate the policy rewrite to the most junior security analyst to save the CISO's time
cards.answer: Initiate a comprehensive policy review and update cycle, establish a recurring review schedule (e.g., annual), and ensure the updated policy covers current technologies, cloud, BYOD, and emerging threats
cards.explanation_correct: An outdated policy is a governance failure — it provides false assurance of control. The CISO should: (1) Review and update the policy to reflect current technology and threat landscape. (2) Establish a recurring review cycle (annually or upon major change) to prevent future drift. (3) Cover cloud, mobile, BYOD, and remote work explicitly. A policy that doesn't reflect reality cannot guide effective security decisions and provides no legal or audit protection.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B creates a gap period with no policy at all — risky and unnecessary. Option C fragments governance by having multiple disconnected documents instead of one coherent policy. Option D delegates a strategic governance task to junior staff who lack the authority and organizational context to write an enforceable policy.

cards.question_text: An organization's acceptable use policy (AUP) states that employees must not install unapproved software. An audit reveals that 40% of employees regularly install utilities and browser extensions. When questioned, managers say they unofficially approve tools verbally but never document it. What governance gap does this reveal?
choices: The AUP lacks an enforceable, documented exception/approval process — without a formal workflow, the policy is unenforceable in practice and managers are creating undocumented risk
The AUP is too restrictive and should allow employees to install any software they want
The problem is that the audit was conducted — audits should not check policy compliance
The IT department should block all USB ports and internet access to prevent installations
cards.answer: The AUP lacks an enforceable, documented exception/approval process — without a formal workflow, the policy is unenforceable in practice and managers are creating undocumented risk
cards.explanation_correct: A policy without an enforcement and exception mechanism creates a culture of non-compliance. The fix is: (1) Create a documented software approval workflow (ticket-based, with risk assessment). (2) Train managers on the process — verbal approvals are not governance. (3) Implement technical controls (application whitelisting or EDR) to enforce the policy. (4) Track exceptions and review them periodically. Policies must be enforceable to have value.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B removes all controls — unrestricted software installation is a major malware risk. Option C is anti-governance — audits are how you verify policy effectiveness. Option D is a blunt technical control that doesn't address the governance gap and would harm productivity.

cards.question_text: A multinational company has a security policy written by HQ in the US. Its European subsidiary must comply with GDPR, which has stricter data protection requirements. The Asian subsidiary has different breach notification laws. The current policy does not account for these regional differences, and the European office has been following local practice instead of HQ policy. What is the best governance approach to resolve this?
choices: Adopt a tiered governance model: a global baseline policy establishing minimum standards, supplemented by regional addenda that address local legal requirements (GDPR, PDPA, etc.), with a central governance body that reviews and harmonizes all variants
Force all subsidiaries to follow the US HQ policy exactly, overriding local laws
Let each subsidiary write its own completely independent policy with no central oversight
Eliminate the global policy and replace it with a single GDPR-compliant policy applied worldwide
cards.answer: Adopt a tiered governance model: a global baseline policy establishing minimum standards, supplemented by regional addenda that address local legal requirements (GDPR, PDPA, etc.), with a central governance body that reviews and harmonizes all variants
cards.explanation_correct: Multinational governance requires balancing global consistency with local compliance. A tiered model works: (1) Global baseline policy sets minimum security standards applicable everywhere. (2) Regional addenda address local legal requirements that exceed the baseline (GDPR's 72-hour breach notification, data residency rules, right to erasure). (3) A central governance body (security steering committee) reviews all variants to ensure no regional policy weakens the global baseline. (4) Local security officers own the regional addenda. This ensures both consistency and compliance.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B creates legal liability — local laws override corporate policy, and non-compliance can result in massive fines (GDPR: up to 4% of global revenue). Option C creates fragmentation and gaps — no central oversight means standards vary wildly. Option D over-applies European requirements globally, which may be unnecessary or conflicting in other jurisdictions.

cards.question_text: What is the difference between an asset, a threat, and a vulnerability in risk management?
choices: An asset is what you want to protect; a threat is a potential danger that can exploit a vulnerability; a vulnerability is a weakness that allows a threat to cause harm
An asset is a type of malware; a threat is a firewall rule; a vulnerability is a patch
A threat is what you want to protect; an asset is a weakness; a vulnerability is a danger
All three terms describe the same concept from different angles
cards.answer: An asset is what you want to protect; a threat is a potential danger that can exploit a vulnerability; a vulnerability is a weakness that allows a threat to cause harm
cards.explanation_correct: These are the building blocks of risk: (1) Asset — anything of value (data, systems, reputation, hardware). (2) Threat — any potential danger (hacker, natural disaster, insider, malware) that could exploit a vulnerability. (3) Vulnerability — a weakness (unpatched software, misconfiguration, weak password, lack of training) that a threat can exploit. Risk exists when a threat has the capability and opportunity to exploit a vulnerability affecting an asset.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B reverses and misdefines all terms — an asset is not malware, a threat is not a firewall rule. Option C scrambles the definitions. Option D is incorrect — they are distinct concepts with specific roles in the risk equation.

cards.question_text: What is Annualized Loss Expectancy (ALE) and how is it calculated?
choices: ALE = SLE × ARO, where SLE is the financial loss from a single occurrence and ARO is the estimated frequency per year
ALE = Total revenue divided by number of security incidents per year
ALE = The cost of all security controls multiplied by the number of employees
ALE = SLE divided by ARO, giving the cost per incident
cards.answer: ALE = SLE × ARO, where SLE is the financial loss from a single occurrence and ARO is the estimated frequency per year
cards.explanation_correct: ALE quantifies expected annual financial loss from a risk. SLE (Single Loss Expectancy) = asset value × exposure factor (percentage of asset lost per incident). ARO (Annualized Rate of Occurrence) = how many times per year the event is expected. Example: If a breach costs $100,000 (SLE) and is expected once every 5 years (ARO = 0.2), ALE = $100,000 × 0.2 = $20,000/year. This helps compare risk against control costs for investment decisions.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B is not a valid risk formula. Option C conflates control costs with risk. Option D divides instead of multiplies — ALE is the product of SLE and ARO, not the quotient.

cards.question_text: A company's risk register lists 50 risks. The CISO has budget to remediate only 10 this quarter. The risks are rated by likelihood and impact on a 1-5 scale. Which approach ensures the most risk reduction per dollar spent?
choices: Prioritize by risk score (likelihood × impact), but adjust for cost-effectiveness: remediate risks where the reduction in ALE per dollar spent is highest, considering both score and remediation cost
Remediate the 10 risks with the highest impact rating regardless of likelihood or cost
Remediate the 10 risks with the highest likelihood rating regardless of impact or cost
Remediate the 10 cheapest risks to maximize the number of risks addressed
cards.answer: Prioritize by risk score (likelihood × impact), but adjust for cost-effectiveness: remediate risks where the reduction in ALE per dollar spent is highest, considering both score and remediation cost
cards.explanation_correct: Risk prioritization should consider: (1) Risk score (likelihood × impact) to identify the most significant risks. (2) Cost-effectiveness — a risk scoring 20 that costs $500K to fix may be lower priority than a risk scoring 16 that costs $50K to fix. (3) The goal is maximizing total risk reduction per dollar. This is essentially an optimization problem: maximize Σ(risk reduction) subject to budget constraint. A risk matrix alone doesn't account for remediation cost.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B ignores likelihood — a high-impact, very unlikely risk may be lower priority than a medium-impact, near-certain risk. Option C ignores impact — a frequent but trivial risk wastes budget. Option D optimizes for quantity over impact — fixing 10 trivial risks may reduce less total risk than fixing 3 critical ones.

cards.question_text: A startup stores customer credit card data and is subject to PCI-DSS. A risk assessment identifies that their payment page has a moderate-risk XSS vulnerability. The startup cannot afford to fix it immediately. Which compensating control would BEST reduce the risk in the interim?
choices: Deploy a Web Application Firewall (WAF) with XSS filtering rules, implement Content Security Policy (CSP) headers, and add output encoding on user input fields — these reduce XSS exploitability while the code fix is pending
Accept the risk since the vulnerability is only moderate severity
Shut down the payment page entirely until the vulnerability can be patched
Transfer the risk by purchasing cyber insurance and taking no technical action
cards.answer: Deploy a Web Application Firewall (WAF) with XSS filtering rules, implement Content Security Policy (CSP) headers, and add output encoding on user input fields — these reduce XSS exploitability while the code fix is pending
cards.explanation_correct: Compensating controls reduce risk when a primary control (code fix) is delayed. For XSS: (1) WAF with XSS signatures blocks malicious input at the perimeter. (2) CSP headers restrict script execution sources, mitigating XSS impact. (3) Output encoding neutralizes malicious payloads. These don't fix the vulnerability but significantly reduce exploitability and impact. The code fix should still be scheduled with an SLA.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B is pure risk acceptance — inappropriate for PCI-DSS compliance where vulnerabilities must be remediated within defined timeframes. Option C is risk avoidance — shutting down the payment page stops revenue, which is disproportionate for a moderate vulnerability. Option D is risk transference — insurance covers financial loss but doesn't reduce the actual vulnerability or protect customer data.

cards.question_text: A company calculates the following for its customer database breach risk: Asset value = $5,000,000. Exposure factor = 40% (40% of data would be compromised in a breach). SLE = $2,000,000. ARO = 0.3 (breach every ~3.3 years). ALE = $600,000. A proposed DLP + encryption + access monitoring solution costs $200,000/year and would reduce the exposure factor to 10% and ARO to 0.1. Calculate the new ALE, the risk reduction value, and determine if the control is cost-effective.
choices: New SLE = $5,000,000 × 10% = $500,000. New ALE = $500,000 × 0.1 = $50,000. Risk reduction = $600,000 - $50,000 = $550,000. Control cost = $200,000. Net benefit = $350,000/year — the control IS cost-effective
New ALE = $600,000. The control does not change the asset value so ALE stays the same
New ALE = $2,000,000 × 0.1 = $200,000. Risk reduction = $400,000. Control cost = $200,000. Net benefit = $200,000 — cost-effective
New ALE = $5,000,000 × 0.1 = $500,000. Risk reduction = $100,000. Control cost = $200,000. Not cost-effective
cards.answer: New SLE = $5,000,000 × 10% = $500,000. New ALE = $500,000 × 0.1 = $50,000. Risk reduction = $600,000 - $50,000 = $550,000. Control cost = $200,000. Net benefit = $350,000/year — the control IS cost-effective
cards.explanation_correct: Step by step: (1) New SLE = Asset value × new exposure factor = $5,000,000 × 10% = $500,000. (2) New ALE = new SLE × new ARO = $500,000 × 0.1 = $50,000. (3) Original ALE = $600,000. (4) Risk reduction = $600,000 - $50,000 = $550,000/year. (5) Control cost = $200,000/year. (6) Net benefit = $550,000 - $200,000 = $350,000/year. The control saves $3.50 in expected losses for every $1 spent — clearly cost-effective.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B misunderstands ALE — both exposure factor and ARO changed, so SLE and ALE both change. Option C uses the old SLE ($2,000,000) instead of recalculating with the new exposure factor. Option D calculates new ALE as asset value × ARO, skipping the exposure factor entirely and using the wrong formula.

cards.question_text: What is the difference between black-box, gray-box, and white-box penetration testing?
choices: Black-box: tester has no prior knowledge; gray-box: tester has partial knowledge (e.g., some credentials or architecture info); white-box: tester has full access to source code, documentation, and internal systems
Black-box: tester uses only automated tools; gray-box: tester uses manual techniques; white-box: tester uses both
Black-box: testing at night; gray-box: testing at dawn; white-box: testing during business hours
Black-box: tests network security only; gray-box: tests application security only; white-box: tests physical security only
cards.answer: Black-box: tester has no prior knowledge; gray-box: tester has partial knowledge (e.g., some credentials or architecture info); white-box: tester has full access to source code, documentation, and internal systems
cards.explanation_correct: The box color refers to the tester's level of prior knowledge: Black-box simulates an external attacker with no insider information — most realistic but may miss internal vulnerabilities. Gray-box provides limited context (user credentials, network diagrams) — balances realism with efficiency. White-box gives full access to source code and architecture — most thorough, finds deep vulnerabilities, but less realistic for external threat simulation. Each has different value depending on the assessment goal.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B confuses test methodology with knowledge level — the box model is about information access, not tools used. Option C is nonsensical — time of day is irrelevant. Option D incorrectly limits each type to a specific security domain — all three can test any layer.

cards.question_text: What is the purpose of a SOC 2 Type II audit, and how does it differ from a SOC 2 Type I audit?
choices: Type II evaluates the design AND operating effectiveness of controls over a period of time (typically 6-12 months); Type I evaluates only the design of controls at a single point in time
Type II is for financial audits; Type I is for security audits
Type II is performed by internal staff; Type I is performed by external auditors
Type II is required by law; Type I is voluntary
cards.answer: Type II evaluates the design AND operating effectiveness of controls over a period of time (typically 6-12 months); Type I evaluates only the design of controls at a single point in time
cards.explanation_correct: SOC 2 audits assess controls related to the Trust Services Criteria (Security, Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality, Privacy). Type I is a point-in-time assessment — it verifies that controls are suitably designed as of a specific date. Type II goes further — it tests whether controls actually operated effectively over a period (usually 6-12 months), providing stronger assurance. Customers and partners typically require Type II because it demonstrates sustained control effectiveness, not just a snapshot.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B is incorrect — both are security/operational audits, not financial (SOC 1 covers financial reporting controls). Option C is wrong — both types must be performed by independent CPAs. Option D is incorrect — neither is legally required; they are driven by customer/vendor requirements and contractual obligations.

cards.question_text: A company conducts an internal vulnerability scan and finds 300 vulnerabilities. Before remediation, management asks the security team to validate which vulnerabilities are actually exploitable. What approach should the team take to efficiently prioritize remediation?
choices: Perform authenticated scanning and risk-based validation: correlate vulnerabilities with asset criticality and exposure, use exploit databases (CVE/EPSS) to check active exploitability, and prioritize vulnerabilities that are exploitable on internet-facing critical assets
Patch all 300 vulnerabilities immediately in order of CVSS score from highest to lowest
Ignore the findings since they were found by an internal scan and not an external attacker
Only fix vulnerabilities that have been actively exploited in the wild, ignoring all others
cards.answer: Perform authenticated scanning and risk-based validation: correlate vulnerabilities with asset criticality and exposure, use exploit databases (CVE/EPSS) to check active exploitability, and prioritize vulnerabilities that are exploitable on internet-facing critical assets
cards.explanation_correct: Not all 300 vulnerabilities are equal. Risk-based validation: (1) Authenticated scanning provides deeper, more accurate results (logged-in scans find more vulnerabilities and reduce false positives). (2) Cross-reference with exploit databases (CVE, EPSS, CISA KEV) to identify actively exploitable vulnerabilities. (3) Correlate with asset criticality — a CVSS 7.0 on a public-facing web server is higher priority than a CVSS 9.0 on an isolated test VM. (4) Consider exposure (internet-facing vs. internal-only). This ensures the most dangerous vulnerabilities are fixed first.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B is inefficient — blindly patching by CVSS score ignores context and may waste effort on low-risk vulnerabilities. Option C is dangerous — internal scans identify real weaknesses that attackers could exploit if they gain access. Option D is too narrow — vulnerabilities without known active exploitation can still be leveraged, especially in targeted attacks.

cards.question_text: An organization wants to assess how well its security team would respond to a real attack. They hire a red team to simulate a sophisticated attack, and a blue team to defend. After the exercise, both teams meet to discuss what happened. What is this exercise called, and what is the meeting's purpose?
choices: A purple team exercise — the red team simulates attacks, the blue team defends, and the joint meeting (purple teaming) shares findings to improve detection and response capabilities through collaborative learning
A black-box penetration test — the meeting is to present the vulnerability report to management
A compliance audit — the meeting is to determine if the organization meets regulatory requirements
A tabletop exercise — the meeting is to discuss a hypothetical scenario without any actual testing
cards.answer: A purple team exercise — the red team simulates attacks, the blue team defends, and the joint meeting (purple teaming) shares findings to improve detection and response capabilities through collaborative learning
cards.explanation_correct: Purple teaming combines red team (offensive) and blue team (defensive) activities into a collaborative learning exercise. The red team attacks using realistic adversary techniques (TTPs). The blue team attempts to detect and respond. Afterward, both sides share their perspectives — the red team reveals what attacks succeeded and why, the blue team explains what they detected and what they missed. This joint debrief (the 'purple' session) transforms adversarial findings into actionable improvements for detection rules, response procedures, and security gaps.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B describes a standard penetration test, which is adversarial and one-directional — the red team reports to the client, not to the blue team. Option C is a compliance activity, not a security exercise. Option D describes a tabletop exercise, which is discussion-based and involves no actual technical testing.

cards.question_text: A SaaS company is preparing for its first SOC 2 Type II audit. The auditor requests evidence that access reviews were performed quarterly for the past 12 months. The company has been doing access reviews but only documented the most recent one — the prior three were done informally via email threads that have since been deleted. The auditor also finds that two developers had admin access to production databases without documented approval. How should the company address these findings, and what does it mean for the audit?
choices: The company should acknowledge the documentation gaps, implement a formal access review process with automated logging and ticket-based approval for privileged access, and accept that the auditor will note these as exceptions in the SOC 2 report for the period when controls were not fully operating effectively
The company should fabricate access review records for the prior quarters to show the auditor
The company should cancel the SOC 2 audit and wait a full year until they have complete documentation
The company should fire the two developers who had admin access as punishment
cards.answer: The company should acknowledge the documentation gaps, implement a formal access review process with automated logging and ticket-based approval for privileged access, and accept that the auditor will note these as exceptions in the SOC 2 report for the period when controls were not fully operating effectively
cards.explanation_correct: SOC 2 Type II requires evidence that controls operated effectively throughout the entire period. Missing documentation means the auditor cannot verify control effectiveness for those quarters — these will be noted as exceptions in the report. The company should: (1) Be transparent — do not hide or fabricate evidence. (2) Implement remediation: automated access review tooling (e.g., IGA solutions), ticket-based privileged access approval workflow, and immutable audit logs. (3) Communicate the remediation plan to the auditor and report users. Exceptions in a SOC 2 report are not necessarily fatal — they are disclosed so users can assess residual risk. Honesty preserves trust; fabrication destroys it.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B is fraud — fabricating audit evidence is illegal and can result in criminal charges, loss of CPA license for the auditor, and complete loss of trust. Option C is overly drastic — the audit can proceed with noted exceptions, and the company can demonstrate remediation going forward. Option D is punitive and misses the systemic issue — the problem is the lack of a formal approval process, not individual misconduct.

cards.question_text: What is social engineering in the context of cybersecurity, and why is it a significant threat?
choices: Social engineering is the manipulation of people into performing actions or divulging confidential information through psychological tricks — it is significant because no technical control can fully prevent a human from being deceived
Social engineering is the process of engineering social media algorithms to block malicious content
Social engineering is a type of network attack that exploits social media APIs
Social engineering is the practice of hiring engineers through social media recruitment
cards.answer: Social engineering is the manipulation of people into performing actions or divulging confidential information through psychological tricks — it is significant because no technical control can fully prevent a human from being deceived
cards.explanation_correct: Social engineering exploits human psychology rather than technical vulnerabilities. Techniques include phishing, pretexting, baiting, tailgating, and quid pro quo. It is dangerous because: (1) Humans are unpredictable — even strong technical controls can be bypassed by a deceived employee. (2) Attackers exploit trust, authority, urgency, and curiosity. (3) It is often the first step in a larger attack (credential theft → network access → data exfiltration). This is why security awareness training is critical — it targets the human layer that technology cannot fully protect.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B describes content moderation, not social engineering. Option C confuses social engineering with API exploitation — it is a human-targeted attack, not a technical one. Option D is about recruitment, completely unrelated to cybersecurity.

cards.question_text: What is the difference between phishing, spear phishing, and whaling?
choices: Phishing: broad, untargeted emails to many recipients; spear phishing: targeted emails aimed at specific individuals or organizations; whaling: spear phishing targeting high-profile executives (CEO, CFO) or individuals with access to valuable assets
Phishing: emails about fishing; spear phishing: emails about fishing with spears; whaling: emails about whale watching
Phishing: attacks via phone; spear phishing: attacks via email; whaling: attacks via SMS
Phishing: low-risk attacks; spear phishing: medium-risk attacks; whaling: high-risk attacks based on technical severity
cards.answer: Phishing: broad, untargeted emails to many recipients; spear phishing: targeted emails aimed at specific individuals or organizations; whaling: spear phishing targeting high-profile executives (CEO, CFO) or individuals with access to valuable assets
cards.explanation_correct: These are tiers of social engineering via email: Phishing casts a wide net (mass emails impersonating banks, delivery services) — low effort, low success rate, high volume. Spear phishing targets specific individuals using personal info (name, role, company) — higher effort, higher success rate. Whaling targets executives or high-value individuals (CEO fraud, wire fraud) — highest effort, highest potential payoff. The defense strategy differs: phishing is blocked by email filters, spear phishing requires user awareness training, whaling requires executive-specific training and financial verification protocols.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B is a literal interpretation of the fishing terms — incorrect. Option C confuses the attack vector — all three are primarily email-based (vishing is phone-based, smishing is SMS-based). Option D categorizes by technical risk severity, which is not how these terms are defined — they are defined by targeting specificity.

cards.question_text: An employee receives a phone call from someone claiming to be from the IT help desk. The caller says there is a urgent security issue with the employee's account and asks for their password to 'verify' the problem. The caller knows the employee's name, department, and manager's name. What type of attack is this, and what should the employee do?
choices: This is vishing (voice phishing) with pretexting — the caller used personal details to build credibility. The employee should not share any credentials, hang up, and report the call to the security team, then verify by calling the IT help desk through the official number
This is a legitimate IT call and the employee should provide their password to help resolve the urgent issue
This is a spam call but harmless — the employee should simply hang up and not report it
This is a physical security threat and the employee should lock their office door
cards.answer: This is vishing (voice phishing) with pretexting — the caller used personal details to build credibility. The employee should not share any credentials, hang up, and report the call to the security team, then verify by calling the IT help desk through the official number
cards.explanation_correct: Vishing (voice phishing) uses phone calls to manipulate victims. Pretexting creates a believable scenario (fake IT help desk) using gathered personal information (name, department, manager) to build trust. The employee should: (1) Never share passwords — legitimate IT staff never ask for them. (2) Hang up and report the incident to security. (3) Verify by calling the IT help desk using the official number from the company directory, not any number provided by the caller. This is why awareness training must cover voice-based social engineering, not just email phishing.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B is exactly what the attacker wants — sharing a password gives full account access. Legitimate IT never asks for passwords. Option C underestimates the threat — vishing can lead to account compromise and should always be reported so security can warn other employees. Option D misidentifies the attack — it is a social engineering phone call, not a physical security issue.

cards.question_text: A company implements a new policy: any employee who fails three phishing simulations in a year will be terminated. After 6 months, the click rate has dropped from 30% to 5%, but the reporting rate has also dropped from 15% to 2%, and employees are deleting suspicious emails without reporting them. What is wrong with this approach, and what should be changed?
choices: The punitive policy created a culture of fear — employees hide failures instead of reporting. The company should replace termination threats with a no-blame learning culture, reward reporting, and focus on education rather than punishment
The policy is working perfectly — a 5% click rate is excellent and the low reporting rate means employees are handling threats independently
The company should increase the threshold to termination after one failure to eliminate all clickers
The company should stop phishing simulations entirely since the click rate is already low
cards.answer: The punitive policy created a culture of fear — employees hide failures instead of reporting. The company should replace termination threats with a no-blame learning culture, reward reporting, and focus on education rather than punishment
cards.explanation_correct: The declining reporting rate is a red flag. Fear-based policies cause employees to: (1) Delete suspicious emails silently to avoid being flagged as a failure — this means real threats go unreported. (2) Not report actual security incidents for fear of blame. (3) Lose trust in the security team. The fix: (1) Replace punishment with immediate, constructive feedback for failed simulations. (2) Actively reward and recognize employees who report phishing (gamification, leaderboards, shout-outs). (3) Make reporting easy (one-click 'Report Phishing' button). A strong reporting culture is more valuable than a low click rate — reports enable the security team to identify campaigns and protect all employees.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B misreads the metrics — a low reporting rate is dangerous because the SOC loses visibility into active threats. Option C would worsen the fear culture and drive reporting rates even lower. Option D is premature — simulations should continue but be paired with a positive, learning-focused approach.

cards.question_text: A hospital's security awareness program shows strong metrics: phishing click rate at 4%, reporting rate at 60%, and mandatory annual training completion at 100%. However, a recent incident revealed that a nurse plugged in a USB drive found in the parking lot, which installed ransomware that encrypted patient records. The nurse had passed all phishing simulations and completed training. The training program never covered physical media threats or removable device policies. What does this reveal, and how should the program be improved?
choices: The program has a coverage gap — it focuses on email phishing but neglects other attack vectors. The hospital should expand training to cover USB/removable media threats, implement technical controls (endpoint policies blocking unauthorized USB devices), add physical security scenarios to simulations (e.g., dropped USB drives in parking lots), and conduct regular threat-landscape reviews to identify emerging vectors
The nurse should be fired for plugging in an unknown USB drive — the training was adequate and this was individual negligence
The hospital should ban all USB drives permanently and physically epoxy all USB ports on all computers
The security awareness program has completely failed and should be rebuilt from scratch
cards.answer: The program has a coverage gap — it focuses on email phishing but neglects other attack vectors. The hospital should expand training to cover USB/removable media threats, implement technical controls (endpoint policies blocking unauthorized USB devices), add physical security scenarios to simulations (e.g., dropped USB drives in parking lots), and conduct regular threat-landscape reviews to identify emerging vectors
cards.explanation_correct: This is a coverage gap, not a total failure. The email phishing program is working well (4% click, 60% report). But awareness training must cover the full threat landscape, not just email. The improvements: (1) Training modules on physical attack vectors — USB drops, tailgating, shoulder surfing, dumpster diving. (2) Technical controls — endpoint DLP/Device Control policies that block or restrict unauthorized USB devices (allow only encrypted, company-issued drives). (3) Physical simulations — drop harmless USB drives in the parking lot and track who plugs them in, then provide immediate education. (4) Regular threat-landscape reviews to ensure training covers emerging attack vectors. Healthcare is especially vulnerable because patient safety depends on system availability.
cards.explanation_wrong_common: Option B is punitive and unfair — the nurse was never trained on this threat vector. Firing one person doesn't prevent the next incident. Option C is excessive — epoxying ports prevents legitimate use (medical devices, equipment updates) and doesn't address the awareness gap. Option D overreacts — the phishing metrics show the program is effective for its covered scope; the issue is coverage, not fundamental failure.
